summary: This memo explains how protocol standards were adopted for the ARPA Internet and the DARPA research community. It covers the process, the authority, and the relationship between the DARPA and DDN communities. It is a policy statement.

eli5.summary: This note describes who decides which network rules become official and how they decide. It is like the rules for making the rules.

questions: how were arpa internet protocol standards adopted
how were early internet protocols approved
role of darpa in internet governance
subtitle: How the Internet research community adopted official protocol standards.

tldr.problem: As the experimental ARPANET and Internet grew, there was no clear process or authority for deciding which protocols became official standards.
tldr.mechanism: DARPA established the Internet Configuration Control Board (ICCB) to oversee the ARPA-Internet, while the Defense Data Network (DDN) community had its own path through military protocol committees. The two communities cooperate but operate under different governance structures.
tldr.outcome: A dual governance model emerged: ICCB advises DARPA on standards for research networks, while the DDN Program Management Office sets policy for operational military networks. Both communities publish official standards in RFCs.

today: RFC 902 documents the governance structure of the 1980s Internet. The ICCB evolved into the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and later the IETF, which became the primary standards body for the Internet. The dual-authority model with DARPA and DoD eventually merged as the military adopted civilian Internet infrastructure.

sections.title: Two Communities, Two Paths
sections.content:
By 1984, the Internet had split into two distinct communities with different needs. The DARPA research community ran the experimental ARPANET, SATNET, and Packet Radio Networks, using them to test new ideas. The Defense Data Network (DDN) was an operational network for DoD use, integrating established systems.

DARPA delegated governance of the ARPA-Internet to the Internet Configuration Control Board (ICCB), a group of researchers representing diverse interests. The DDN had its own hierarchy of policy committees and a Program Management Office that enforced standards. The challenge was coordinating the two without either controlling the other.
sections.eli5: A lab wanted to experiment with new ideas, while the military needed reliable, tested rules. Both used the same network but for different reasons.

sections.title: How a Protocol Becomes Official
sections.content:
A typical path to standardization began with informal discussion, moved to a draft proposal reviewed by interested parties, and eventually became a formal RFC for broad comment. If the ICCB deemed a protocol promising, it could authorize test implementations with a handful of participants. Only after testing was complete and the protocol refined did the ICCB recommend it as official, announced in an RFC with a clear policy statement.

Lower-level protocols (like TCP) were subject to more rigorous review than higher-level protocols (like email utilities). The RFC Editor, Jon Postel, coordinated the publication of all protocol definitions and maintained the 'Official Protocols' list (RFC 901 at the time) documenting each protocol's status, specification, and dependencies.
sections.eli5: An idea gets written down, people argue about it, a few try to build it, problems get fixed, and finally it becomes official—if it works.

sections.title: Cooperation Despite Separation
sections.content:
The DARPA and DDN worlds maintained separate authority but shared personnel and working relationships. A few individuals served on both the ICCB and military committees, and technical people at lower levels worked together. When the ICCB decided a protocol should be adopted, the DDN could independently decide to adopt it on the same schedule, wait for experimental results, or decline entirely.

TCP, for example, had two official specifications: RFC 793 for the DARPA research community and Military Standard 1778 for the DDN. Both defined the same protocol but through separate governance paths.
sections.eli5: Two organizations could use the same tool if they both agreed it was good, but either could decide on their own timeline.

references.text: Postel, J. and Reynolds, J., "Official Protocols", RFC 901, June 1984.
